title: I work, she works — present simple
learningObjective: Describe habits, routines, facts and preferences using positive present simple forms and frequency words.
hook: She is cooking now. She cooks every evening.
script:
In Unit 3, she is cooking describes an action now. Today we will describe what she does regularly: she cooks every evening.

Watch dinner appear across the week. She cooks every evening describes a repeated habit, not just this moment.

We call this the present simple. It describes what is regularly or generally true. Habits repeat. Routines are the usual order of activities. We also use it for facts and preferences.

Nora wakes up at seven, eats breakfast at eight, and starts work at nine. These pictures show her usual morning. They do not mean all three actions are happening now.

Birds have feathers. This sentence states a general fact. It is not a description of a special action happening as we speak.

He likes basketball. We describe his interest, not one action now. Like names a preference. Present simple verbs can describe what someone likes or enjoys.

I work at a hospital describes my regular job. I can say it while I am at home. The sentence does not mean I am working at this exact moment.

Use a subject, the main verb, and any other information. In I drink tea, drink carries the main meaning. Here it names the activity.

With I, you, we and they, use the base form: the ordinary dictionary form. I play basketball. You speak English. The verb has no extra s in these examples.

We live near the city. They enjoy music. Live and enjoy stay in their base form with we and they. Choose the subject before changing the verb.

English uses a different verb form with he, she and it in these positive statements. I work, but he works. The added s matches he; it does not mean several actions.

She plays tennis. It lives in the garden, for example a small bird. She and it follow the same verb pattern as he. Usually add s or es to the base form.

Daniel is one person we can call he. Daniel works at a restaurant. A single name or noun like my brother follows the he or she pattern.

I means one speaker, but we still say I work, not I works. You work is correct for one listener or several. The s rule is for the he, she and it group.

For most verbs, add s with he, she or it. Work becomes works, read becomes reads, and play becomes plays.

After endings such as ch, sh and ss in these verbs, add es. Watch becomes watches, finish becomes finishes, and pass becomes passes.

Go and do take es in this group: she goes, he does. My sister goes to the gym. He does his homework after dinner. Here do names the activity.

I have a bicycle becomes she has a bicycle. Have has a special form: has. Learn it as a pair; do not add s to make haves.

A, e, i, o and u are vowel letters; d and r here are consonants. Study ends in consonant plus y. Change y to ies: studies. Try becomes tries.

In play, the letter before y is a, a vowel. Keep y and add s: plays. Enjoy also has a vowel before y: enjoys. Not every verb ending in y changes to ies.

She studies in the evening. He tries again. The spelling has changed, but the verb still describes a regular activity. Match both subject and spelling.

Frequency words tell us how often an activity happens. We will compare example weeks. The pictures illustrate meanings; they are not fixed counts or percentages.

Always means every time in the situation we mean. Maya always cooks dinner. Every day is marked in this example week.

Usually means this is the normal pattern, with exceptions. Maya usually cooks dinner. Most days follow her usual routine.

Often means an activity happens many times. Maya often cooks dinner. We are describing something frequent, not giving an exact number.

Sometimes means on some occasions, but not all the time. Maya sometimes cooks dinner. Some days show the activity; others do not.

Never means not on any occasion in the situation we mean. Maya never cooks dinner. No day shows cooking in this example.

I always brush my teeth before bed. She usually walks to work. We often cook together. These words describe the regular pattern.

They sometimes visit the beach. He never drinks coffee. Never already gives a negative meaning. For now, learn this useful frequency-word pattern as it stands.

In our ordinary main-verb examples, put the frequency word before the main verb. She always studies in the evening. Always comes before studies.

She studies always in the evening is not our ordinary word order. Move always before studies: she always studies in the evening.

I drink never soda puts never after the main verb. Say I never drink soda. Never comes before drink in the pattern we are practising.

This position rule describes the ordinary main verbs in today’s examples. The verb be has a different usual pattern. We are not learning all placement exceptions here.

I ___ near the park. [Pause five seconds.] Live. With I, use the base form live.

She ___ to school. [Pause five seconds.] Walks. She takes the s form: walks.

He ___ birds. (watch) [Pause five seconds.] Watches. Watch ends in ch: add es.

Maya ___ after dinner. (study) [Pause five seconds.] Studies. A consonant before y gives studies.

He ___ chess. (play) [Pause five seconds.] Plays. A vowel before y: keep y and add s.

My sister ___ a bicycle. [Pause five seconds.] Has. My sister means she: use has.

He ___ homework at six. [Pause five seconds.] Does. With he, the activity verb do becomes does.

Nora works in a shop. This describes… [Pause five seconds.] Her regular job. Present simple can describe regular work.

On every visit, I bring a book. I ___ bring a book. [Pause five seconds.] Always. Always means every time here.

Not on any occasion: he ___ drinks coffee. [Pause five seconds.] Never. Never means not on any occasion.

Put often before the main verb. [Pause five seconds.] She often reads. Often goes before the main verb reads.

Look at the bowl beside eight am on Nora’s schedule. Use the picture and the time in the next sentence to describe her routine.

At eight, Nora, blank, breakfast. [Pause five seconds.] Eats. Nora means she: eats matches her routine.

Use present simple for habits, routines, facts and preferences. I, you, we and they use the base form. He, she and it usually need s or es.

Nora usually eats breakfast at eight. Usually goes before eats. Nora matches she, so eat takes s. This sentence describes her routine.
